To address this problem, this paper proposes Z-cache as a feature caching method that can maintain high-quality generation through self-reflection. Concretely, we observe that the error from feature caching tends to be sharply reduced after each full computation. Based on this observation, Z-Cache is designed to first predict the features in the future caching steps and then perform a full computation. After that, Z-Cache returns to the caching steps and re-predicts them based on the previous and the current computation steps, which brings correction in features. Experiments demonstrate that with Z-Cache, diffusion transformers achieve comparable generation quality to the original model but with faster inference speed, for instance, 6.22X acceleration on FLUX-dev for text-to-image generation. Our code is released on GitHub.

title: Biological Congruence: Evaluating Microscopy Generation Across Representations
author: Duway Nicolas Lesmes-Leon
Shumpei Takezaki
Fabian Schmeisser
Ryoma Bise
Gillian Lovell
Bianca Migliori
Andreas Dengel
Sheraz Ahmed
abstract: Generative models increasingly produce realistic microscopy images, yet conventional evaluation primarily characterizes visual fidelity and distributional coverage rather than the biological information represented by synthetic data. We introduce biological congruence as an evaluation principle describing whether biologically relevant information forms a coherent description across representations and remains consistent with its empirical biological context. To study this principle, we develop a text-conditioned diffusion framework that jointly generates microscopy images and instance masks, exposing the same generated biological state through conditioning, visual appearance, and instance structure. Across prompt--mask, prompt--image, image--mask, and population-level analyses, we find strongly feature-dependent behavior: density and confluency are consistently preserved, morphology exhibits recurrent disagreement, while nearest-neighbor distance reveals that strong image--mask agreement can coexist with weaker conditioning and population fidelity. Stress testing increasingly unsupported phenotype combinations further shows that target controllability can increase while untargeted phenotypes reorganize and the complete generated state moves toward configurations better supported by real data. These findings demonstrate that generative quality, controllability, cross-representation agreement, and population fidelity capture complementary properties, motivating biological congruence as a relational perspective for evaluating scientific generative models.

title: Missingness-Aware Prior-Data Fitted Network for Irregular Clinical Time-Series
author: Hadi Mehdizavareh
Gabriele Santangelo
Giovanna Nicora
Pietro Bosoni
Simon Lebech Cichosz
Arianna Dagliati
Arijit Khan
Riccardo Bellazzi
abstract: Clinical time series are irregularly observed with laboratory measurements recorded at uneven intervals and observation patterns often reflecting patient state, clinical concern, and site-specific practice. Consequently, missingness is not merely a nuisance factor but an informative signal for prediction. We propose a Missingness-Aware Prior-Data Fitted Network (MA-PFN) for irregular clinical time-series prediction. MA-PFN first learns a diffusion-based prior over joint laboratory value and observation-mask trajectories from source-domain electronic health records, capturing both physiological dynamics and measurement processes. Synthetic trajectories sampled from this prior are then transformed into context-query tasks to train a PFN-style conditional predictor. Once trained, the model performs prediction for new admissions in a single forward pass, requiring neither retraining nor parameter adaptation on target datasets. The framework naturally supports both imputation and forecasting through different context-query constructions. We conduct internal validation on a held-out MIMIC-III test set and external validation on eICU, evaluating both imputation and forecasting and assessing cross-domain generalization under shifts in patient populations, clinical practices, and observation mechanisms. MA-PFN achieves the best performance across all evaluated settings, with Overall/Macro nRMSD ranging from (0.193/0.186) for internal imputation to (0.297/0.297) for external forecasting, without target-domain adaptation. These results demonstrate that learning missingness-aware task priors enables accurate and transferable clinical time-series prediction under informative missingness.

title: Learning-to-Memorize: Dynamic Context Management for Long-Horizon Autoregressive Video Generation
author: Haowei Zhu
Qijie Wang
Jia Li
Xing Wang
Tianyu Zhao
Jiexi Wang
Xurui Peng
Xinglong Wu
Junhai Yong
Bin Wan
abstract: Autoregressive video generation has achieved impressive results on short clips, yet generating long videos remains challenging due to error accumulation over extended horizons, where each predicted frame depends on potentially imperfect previous frames. Existing approaches typically rely on static context management strategies, such as sliding-window caches that discard early frames or fixed sink frames that permanently preserve initial content. These designs either lose critical long-range context or anchor generation to outdated information, which can lead to degraded fidelity, motion stagnation, and reduced diversity. In this paper, we propose Learning to Memorize (L2M), a learned context memory management framework that dynamically retains, evicts, and evolves historical frames according to predicted importance. The framework consists of an importance prediction router that estimates the relevance of each historical frame, degradation-aware training that improves robustness to noisy or corrupted context, and a dynamic memory initialization and evolution mechanism that updates long-term memory using exponential moving average (EMA) importance scores. This allows high-quality frames to replace stale anchors and enables memory to adapt naturally to scene evolution. Trained with a teacher-student distillation objective and sparsity regularization, L2M makes efficient use of a fixed KV-cache budget while preserving the most informative contextual information. Extensive experiments demonstrate that L2M improves long-horizon video generation quality and temporal consistency over existing baselines, providing a learned strategy for context memory management in long autoregressive video generation.

title: Apto: Self-Adaptive CPU-GPU Hybrid MoE Inference on Shared PCs
author: Zihang Zhong
Jiali Wang
Rong Chen
abstract: CPU/GPU hybrid inference enables Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models to run on memory-constrained PCs by keeping all expert weights in host memory and executing activated experts across both processors. Existing hybrid systems, however, assume exclusive resource access and determine an upfront CPU/GPU partition, so CPU contention from colocated applications can severely imbalance the two execution paths. This paper presents Apto, a self-adaptive hybrid inference system that applies dynamic scheduling to expert execution. The CPU and GPU executors claim experts from opposite ends of a dual-ended queue as they progress, allowing the CPU/GPU work split to adapt to their execution progress without predicting contention. Apto further uses affinity-aware scheduling to expose each executor's preferred experts at its queue end and cancellable tail racing to mitigate final-expert stragglers. Compared with state-of-the-art GPU-only and hybrid baselines, Apto achieves average prefill and decode speedups of 2.96$\times$ and 1.52$\times$ under standalone execution, and 5.97$\times$ and 3.45$\times$ under concurrent CPU workloads. It also accelerates real-world coding-agent applications by 2.02$\times$ on average.

title: Advances in Agentic Computer Graphics
author: Hengyu Liu
Jihyeon Je
Ruiqi Wang
Mingxuan Wu
Haven Feng
Qixing Huang
Georgios Pavlakos
Hao Zhang
Jiajun Wu
Maneesh Agrawala
Leonidas Guibas
R. Kenny Jones
Shangzhe Wu
Guandao Yang
abstract: Computer graphics is built on code. Large language model (LLM) agents can now generate graphics code and iteratively refine it through various feedback. This capability opens the door to a potentially new paradigm of computer graphics, with graphics algorithms increasingly built around agentic systems to automate progressively complex tasks. Over the past years, research on agentic graphics has expanded rapidly across a diverse range of tasks. This rapid growth makes it increasingly difficult for manual literature reviews to keep pace with new developments. At the same time, similar ideas are often described using different terminology across these tasks, further complicating efforts to develop a systematic understanding of the field. In this report, we address these challenges through two contributions. First, we introduce a unified taxonomy for characterizing agentic systems across diverse computer graphics tasks. Second, we develop an agentic literature system that can assist human researchers in analyzing existing and newly published papers at scale. Building on these contributions, we analyze emerging research trends and discuss open challenges in coordinating agents and tools across graphics tasks, designing interfaces and representations for human-agent collaboration, sustaining long-horizon planning and refinement, and reliably evaluating interactive graphics systems.

title: Quantizing Recurrent Language Models Is Easier Than You Think
author: Philipp Nazari
Neehal Tumma
Daniela Rus
T. Konstantin Rusch
abstract: Linear recurrences are becoming an increasingly common building block in large language models, replacing the growing KV cache of softmax attention with a fixed-size recurrent state that enables efficient decoding. However, the quantization stack has largely been developed around softmax Transformers, whose numerical properties and inference state differ from those of recurrent models. Our goal is to understand these differences and study the design space of quantization methods for recurrent models. In our analysis, we differentiate between two targets. First, extra-state quantization concerns weights and activations outside the recurrent state, whose distributions are shaped indirectly by the sequence mixer during training. In controlled 1.3B parameter models, we find that decayed recurrences develop weaker residual outlier channels than softmax attention and are therefore easier to quantize without incoherence processing. Second, intra-state quantization concerns the recurrent state itself during decode, where repeated updates create a different numerical problem from KV cache quantization. We instantiate our findings as LoReS, a state quantization pipeline combining value-axis scale grouping to match output channel magnitude, decay-based mixed-precision to protect slowly decaying heads or channels, and stochastic rounding to limit error accumulation under repeated requantization. Across Qwen-3.5 9B, Nemotron-H 8B, and Kimi-Linear 48B-A3B, LoReS supports robust 8-bit state quantization and lower effective precision on shorter decode horizons. We implement LoReS in vLLM and demonstrate end-to-end decode speedups.

title: Don't Guess, Ask Wisely: Benchmarking and Training Proactive Elicitation in Open-Domain LLM Conversations
author: Rongyu Zhang
Mutian Bao
Jinjian Zhang
Yuetian Du
He Xu
Wei Zhou
Xiaojun Zhu
Ming Kong
Jie Liu
Linjian Mo
Qiang Zhu
abstract: When user queries are incomplete, large language models should ask targeted questions before committing to an answer, a capability we call proactive elicitation, yet evaluation on real user-assistant queries across seven LLMs (8B to frontier) shows that fewer than 11% of underspecified queries trigger a follow-up question. To benchmark and train this capability, we introduce VagueBench, where each seed query is annotated with structured intent and detail units then degraded into intent-vague and fully-vague variants via controlled removal of linguistic cues, yielding known hidden information sets for evaluating both when and what to ask. We propose DialogGRPO, an offline reinforcement learning method that organizes multi-turn elicitation as a dialogue-state directed acyclic graph, where candidate questions at each node receive dense turn-level rewards combining immediate information gain with lookahead value through group-relative comparison, enabling fine-grained credit assignment without runtime simulation. DialogGRPO elicits missing information on over 88% of vague queries with substantial gains in both recovery efficiency and answer coverage, without over-asking on complete queries, outperforms prompting and test-time-scaling baselines, and generalizes zero-shot to MultiWOZ 2.4 and AmbigQA.

title: Who Asks, Who Answers: Linear Attention Builds the Query in Hybrid Language Models
author: Wenqi Zeng
Chen Feng
YuAng Chen
abstract: Hybrid language models interleave linear-attention layers with a small number of softmax-attention layers. Prior work largely attributes in-context retrieval to softmax attention, treating linear attention primarily as a mechanism for compressing past context. We revisit this division of labor and show that linear attention plays a direct role in retrieval by constructing the query used by softmax attention. Studying Qwen3.5 (Gated DeltaNet) and Granite4.0 (Mamba-2), we identify an Encode--Address circuit. An early Encode block preserves token identity, while an Address block constructs the final-position representation from which a softmax \emph{reader} forms its attention query. Transplanting this representation between prompts with different queried keys redirects retrieval in 0.97--0.99 of cases. The Address block's recurrent state carries the retrieval target, and its computation transfers across architectures: replacing Granite's Address block with Qwen's restores retrieval accuracy to 0.92--0.94 without updating either model's weights. Across six Qwen3.5 models, Address computation becomes distributed at larger scales over a chain of blocks, each guiding a successive reader, as the query no longer passes from one reader to the next through attention. These findings reveal a division of labor in hybrid retrieval: linear attention constructs the query, while softmax attention performs the lookup. Code is available at https://github.com/yuang-chen/LinearQuery

title: EAGR: Evidence-Guided Adaptive Graph Retrieval
author: Sonam Gupta
Vignesh P
Vishwajeet Kumar
Adnan Qidwai
Anand Eswaran
Jaydeep Sen
Sachindra Joshi
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) for multi-hop reasoning requires retrieval to adapt as intermediate evidence reveals new information needs. Existing approaches support such retrieval through explicit graph structures or iterative query reformulation, introducing graph-construction or query-time overhead. We present Evidence-Guided Adaptive Graph Retrieval (EAGR), a framework in which accumulated evidence dynamically determines which semantic directions to explore next, and which requires no dedicated graph database and no explicit graph materialization. EAGR operates over an implicit semantic graph induced by compact passage metadata pre-ingested into a standard VectorDB. Starting from dense-retrieval seed passages, an LLM iteratively assesses accumulated evidence, identifies promising semantic directions, expands the retrieval frontier through metadata-based neighborhood lookup, and terminates once sufficient evidence has been collected. By precomputing semantic metadata, EAGR enables evidence-conditioned graph exploration without materializing an explicit graph, maintaining a dedicated GraphDB, or iteratively rewriting the query. Across three widely used multi-hop QA benchmarks, EAGR achieves the highest LLM-based answer accuracy among evaluated methods, outperforming the vanilla RAG by 17\% and strongest graph-aware baseline by 4\% percentage points averaged across three popular benchmarks HotPotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue.

title: AgenticMobility: An Open-Source Platform for Multi-AI-Agent Mobility Dynamics
author: Jiaheng Xiao
Jiangtao Han
Jiachen Wang
Honghai Li
Lijun Sun
Kay Axhausen
Chang Liu
Zhengbing He
abstract:
Understanding mobility dynamics and the effects of urban transportation management policies requires examining how individual travel decisions, traffic conditions, and policy interventions influence one another over time. We present AgenticMobility, an open-source experimental platform for studying how mobility AI agents and other AI agents interact, adapt through repeated experience, and collectively shape mobility outcomes. Persistent agents retain identities and relevant states across rounds, with explicit interfaces defining information access, admissible actions, and decision schedules; linked records trace decisions, execution, and feedback.
In the current implementation, large language model (LLM) agents act as travelers choosing routes and departure times and as a manager periodically adjusting link charges within MATSim. A preliminary demonstration spans 100 simulated days in each of five configurations, with one run per configuration and a shared simulation seed. In the joint traveler--manager run, all 1,179,300 finalized target decisions satisfied action constraints; execution checks verified implementation of accepted choices and preservation of personal memories across days. Trajectories show stable route choices alongside departure-time adjustments and differences between controlled-trip and population-wide outcomes.
The platform supports experiments on individual adaptation, collective outcomes, and management interventions by varying information access, retained experience, and management feedback. Source code is available at https://github.com/Agentic-City-Research/Agentic-Mobility

title: TAC-CoT: Tool-Empowered Implicit Chain-of-Thought via Interleaving Explicit Tokens
author: Juseon Do
Sangmin Bae
Jeesu Jung
Hwanjun Song
abstract: LLM-based agentic systems are increasingly combined with CoT reasoning to solve tasks that require accurate reasoning, external knowledge, and multi-step deliberation. Yet, explicit CoT incurs substantial generation overhead, while implicit CoT, which replaces textual rationales with compact continuous tokens, does not naturally support the explicit communication interface required for agentic tool-use. We propose TAC-CoT, a tool-empowered adaptive implicit CoT framework that replaces explicit reasoning traces with compact latent reasoning segments while retaining textual tokens only for tool calls, observations, and final answers. This interleaved design enables agentic tool-use without verbalizing every intermediate reasoning step. Experiments on agentic math and QA benchmarks show that TAC-CoT improves accuracy by up to 8.8 points while reducing model forward passes by up to 6.8x. Furthermore, analyses show that TAC-CoT improves tool-use quality in both single- and multi-tool settings.

title: Is Your Long-Horizon Benchmark Really Deep? Measuring and Synthesizing Depth in Terminal Tasks
author: Yu Jiang
Yue Huang
Hang Hua
Yuyang Wu
Zixuan Weng
Olexandr Isayev
Yue Zhao
Zinan Lin
Xiangliang Zhang
abstract: Long-horizon terminal tasks are used to evaluate and train agents. Human-curated datasets are scarce, so many synthesis methods have emerged. They usually measure the length of a task by the turns a model needs to pass it, and its difficulty by labels the LLM sets during generation. We find, however, that the turn count largely reflects the habits of the model, not only the demands of the task, and that the labels barely track how often models pass. We describe a terminal task by its work, the number of operations it requires, and its depth, the number of turns that must happen in sequence because the commands of each turn can only be chosen after reading the output of the previous one. Estimating depth as the smallest turn cap, stated to the agent, under which the task passes, we audit 734 tasks from six existing datasets. Synthesis has mostly added work, not depth: 94% of the solved synthetic tasks pass within three turns, yet depth, unlike the turn count, predicts difficulty beyond work. We propose DEPTH, in which a generation agent writes each task one segment at a time in a real software environment, carrying out each segment before writing it and starting the next from the state it leaves. Our 105 tasks exceed every audited dataset in depth and work, and none of six current models passes half of them. Fine-tuning Qwen3-8B on runs from these tasks improves it on two terminal benchmarks.

title: RECEIPT: Measuring and Repairing the Return Assumption of LLM Agents in Web Service Operations
author: Boyang Yang
Ziyao Yang
Yu Zhang
Duo Chai
Xiaoming Chen
Haoye Tian
abstract:
LLM agents operate Web infrastructure from the command line and rely on a return assumption, namely that each tool call returns within a bounded time and with its requested action finished. Many commands, however, ask a question before they act, and the agent's harness either closes the program's input or keeps it open as a terminal at which nobody types. With closed input, the program can return status 0 without the requested action. With open input, it waits until a time limit, and the agent pays in time and tokens. To the best of our knowledge, this paper is the first to measure and repair the return assumption. We collect 91,469 production tool calls and 89,047 public agent trajectories, test how 8 widely used harnesses launch commands, and build Litmus, a catalog of 158 checked command-line invocations, and Tripwire, a benchmark of 25 task pairs that differ only in whether a question guards the requested action. We then propose RECEIPT, which keeps the input open, reads what each process waits for from system calls, and returns this state to an unmodified agent through a model-checked protocol.
On Litmus, closed input causes 11.5% of tested invocations to return status 0 without performing the requested action, and 7 of 8 harnesses close input when no terminal is attached. An unanswered question at a plain terminal multiplies a task's token use by 2.9, and the input connection moves an LLM from 7th to 3rd place among 8. Across 5 LLMs, RECEIPT reduces false claims of success by 73.5% and completes all 25 guarded tasks on a second harness. An agent's reliability therefore depends on what its harness lets it observe as well as on its LLM. Agent builders should report what each tool call did, not only how it ended, and benchmark maintainers should fix and report the input connection before they rank LLMs.

title: TriPhysBench: Evaluating Physical Intelligence for Embodied Agents
author: Zhongxiang Sun
Chenghao Yang
Haojie Ding
Boheng Zhang
Fan Yang
Qingsong Wen
Kun Wang
abstract: Embodied agents need physical intelligence to understand their surroundings through physical perception, physical knowledge retrieval, and physical reasoning. These capabilities must work together to interpret events and make quantitative judgments. Existing benchmarks advance physical understanding and general-purpose tool use, yet the coordination of these capabilities in physical scenarios remains insufficiently characterized. Inspired by Popper's Three Worlds, we introduce TriPhysBench, a benchmark of 410 questions from 200 videos that brings physical perception, physical knowledge retrieval, and physical reasoning into a shared evaluation setting. Its measurement-grounded and knowledge-grounded subtasks impose complementary demands on obtaining observations and acquiring external specifications, then applying them to quantitative problems. Among six representative vision-language models, the best achieves an answer accuracy of only 50.38%, revealing limited performance on tasks that require these capabilities to work together. We further introduce TriPhys, a framework that learns a unified policy for physical perception, knowledge retrieval, and quantitative reasoning from complete tool-integrated trajectories. The policy uses intermediate reasoning to guide retrieval and computation, then incorporates tool feedback into subsequent physical inference. On 110 questions from videos excluded from training, TriPhys improves answer and solution scores across three Qwen configurations, with a 17.7% relative gain in answer accuracy for TriPhys-27B over its Qwen3.6-27B backbone. This work provides a benchmark and a learning pathway toward embodied agents that move beyond recognizing events to understanding and reasoning about the physical processes behind them.

title: No Note Is an Island: Probing LLMs' Understanding of Crowdsourced Fact-Checking Environments
author: Weijian Fan
Chichen Lin
Xiao Han
Jiaying Wu
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly assist crowdsourced fact-checking, yet evaluations focus on individual annotations. A correction's reach and reception depend on visibility, audience responses, and platform policies. We introduce correction context understanding: assessing corrective content, interpreting audience responses, and reasoning about platform dynamics within a shared environment. We build NoteHabitat from 36 months of Weibo Annotations data, linking 102,994 posts (42,853 annotations), 431,407 comments, and five policy events. Evaluating diverse model families across seven tasks spanning content, interaction, and management reveals three gaps. Annotation quality correlates only weakly with engagement ($\rho=0.068$), while four zero-shot LLMs systematically underrate quality relative to human judgments, especially evidence support and objectivity. Models also miss toxic comments supporting corrections (36.4% average recall across ten models). At the platform level, LLMs partially predict policy-associated outcome directions, but LLM-guided simulations poorly reproduce daily activity. Cross-group analyses expose blind spots tied to contribution types and reader stances that aggregate scores conceal. Reliable fact-checking AI must understand the note, the conversation around it, and the platform in which both unfold.

title: Spade-SLAM: Sparse Correspondence Anchors for Dense Self-Supervised Visual SLAM
author: Julian Philipp Schmitt
Weirong Chen
Ganlin Zhang
Felix Wimbauer
Daniel Cremers
abstract: We introduce Spade-SLAM, a self-supervised dense visual SLAM framework that substantially narrows the long-standing performance gap to supervised methods in a zero-shot setting. By demonstrating that high-fidelity tracking can be achieved without explicit ground-truth pose and depth labels, our approach offers a highly effective and label-efficient alternative to fully supervised pretraining. Our core contribution is a complementary sparse-to-dense training regime: While a warping-based photometric loss provides a dense training signal, we stabilize the optimization and suppress drift in ambiguous regions using a sparse correspondence loss derived from image feature matches. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Spade-SLAM significantly improves robustness and accuracy compared to existing self-supervised baselines, closely rivaling SLAM systems trained with explicit pose and depth supervision. The code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/JulianPSchmitt/Spade-SLAM.

title: VLSplat: Vision-Language Guided Object-Centric 3D Gaussian Splatting via Scene Graph
author: Yuntae Jeon
Younho Jeon
Sujin Jin
Sungho Jo
Seunghee Park
abstract: Learning semantic representations for 3D Gaussian Splatting has recently emerged as a promising direction for 3D scene understanding. However, existing 2D-to-3D semantic lifting approaches rely primarily on 2D segmentation supervision and lack object-level priors, causing the learned representation to be driven by local mask evidence rather than holistic object structure. In this paper, we present VLSplat, a vision-language guided approach for object-centric semantic lifting in 3D Gaussian Splatting. Our method augments mask-based lifting with object-level semantic priors derived from vision-language models and refines Gaussian representations using an object-group scene graph. The refinement is performed through two language-guided modules: intra-group refinement suppresses semantic noise within object groups, while inter-group acquisition expands object support regions by incorporating structurally relevant candidates from neighboring groups. Extensive experiments on indoor scene datasets demonstrate that VLSplat improves the semantic consistency and structural completeness of object-level categories. Our code and models are available at https://vlsplat.github.io/.

title: Beyond Multimodal Emotion Conflict: Temporal Context-Aware Hidden Emotion Detection with Multimodal Large Language Models
author: Yonghao Wang
Jiaxin Zhou
abstract: Multimodal emotion recognition commonly combines textual, acoustic, and visual signals to infer affective states. Recent work has begun to study conflicts among modalities, but a conflict does not necessarily indicate that a person is concealing an emotion. It may also result from mixed emotions, individual expressive styles, or contextual factors. This proposal aims to distinguish ordinary emotional inconsistency from emotion concealment and to infer the underlying emotion when supported by evidence. We plan to construct a multimodal benchmark with explicit annotations of expressed emotion, internal emotion, and concealment conditions, and to develop an MLLM-based framework that integrates fine-grained facial Action Units (AUs), cross-modal features, and temporal context.

title: Towards Self-Evolving Narrative Systems: Real-Time Adaptation and Long-Term Optimization with LLMs
author: Ruisheng Sun
Jiaqi Shao
Weijia Han
Linxi Ju
Yunzhen Zhang
Binyan Sun
Rong Chen
Benjamin Blas Maristany
Ye Lu
Rui Hu
Ernesto Escobar
Bing Luo
abstract: Traditional interactive narrative systems offer strong authorial control and structural coherence but often restrict player agency. In contrast, LLM-driven narratives enable open-ended generation and greater flexibility, yet frequently suffer from inconsistency and diminished narrative control. To navigate this trade-off, we propose a hybrid narrative framework that dynamically balances pre-authored content with real-time LLM generation via semantic similarity alignment. Additionally, sustaining narrative quality over extended gameplay remains a core challenge in LLM-based storytelling. To address this, we introduce a self-evolving, feedback-driven optimization framework that leverages in-context learning to iteratively refine prompts, eliminating the need for manual prompt engineering. Through a case study and participant-based evaluation, we show that our framework enhances narrative coherence while preserving player agency, effectively aligning generated content with both authorial intent and evolving player behavior.

title: Object-Only Is Not Context-Free: A Counterfactual Diagnostic for Context Removal in Object Retrieval
author: Boaz Meivar
Shai Avidan
abstract: Object-centric retrieval pipelines often mask the background before pooling backbone features, aiming for a descriptor that reflects the object rather than its scene. Whether this truly yields an object-only descriptor, however, is rarely tested. We introduce the Keyhole Aperture Probe (KAP), a counterfactual diagnostic that repurposes the ground-truth masks of existing panoptic segmentation datasets (COCO, ADE20K) for retrieval: it holds the pooled object region fixed and varies only the pixels outside it, summarizing a backbone's context dependence in a single number. We find that the pooled object region has already integrated its surround. Replacing the context, with a neutral fill or even a different real scene, changes the descriptor, and when retrieval fails under a blank fill, the descriptor matches plain-background images rather than its own object. Object-only is not context-free. Across ten modern backbones, object-only descriptors retain only about a quarter to two-thirds of their full-image accuracy, and the effect is not unique to Transformer self-attention: a convolutional backbone shows it too. The dependence is also reducible: a lightweight adapter that encourages the descriptor to stay stable as context is removed lowers it and improves full-image instance retrieval on INSTRE, transferring to ILIAS with accuracy improved or preserved. A matched contrastive-fine-tuning control does not reproduce those gains. We release KAP as a simple, backbone-agnostic evaluation protocol to measure and reduce this dependence before deployment.

title: Beyond Prompt Injection: The Tool Update Gap in LLM Agent Security
author: Shiyu Kan
Yue Qi
Yufei Han
Xinjian Luo
Guojun Xiong
Xiaofeng Gao
abstract:
Large language model based agents increasingly rely on external tools to invoke services and interact with web resources. These tools can evolve through software updates, yet agentic frameworks may continue trusting them without re-verifying their safety after implementation changes. This tool update gap creates a supply-chain vulnerability in agentic systems: because updated tool code executes outside the LLM's context window, malicious functionality embedded in tool updates can bypass defenses centered on model-visible interactions, leaving agents exposed to stealthy, persistent threats that existing in-context defenses can hardly address.
To thoroughly investigate this threat, we introduce ETUDE (Exploiting Tool Updates for Direct Execution), an attack that embeds malicious functionality into updates of initially benign tools to produce compromised tools, while preserving their legitimate tool functionality. Unlike prompt-based attacks, ETUDE operates entirely outside the LLM's context and requires no adversarial instructions, thereby bypassing defenses restricted to model-visible content. We evaluate ETUDE across three representative attack workloads and seven widely used commercial and open-source agentic frameworks, including Gemini CLI, Codex CLI, and Claude Code. The results show that ETUDE achieves a 97.6% ASR while maintaining a 95.9% legitimate task completion rate.
We further examine existing defenses and find that they provide insufficient protection against this threat. These findings expose a fundamental blind spot in current agent security practices: trust established for a tool does not necessarily remain valid after its implementation updates.

title: RubricWorld: World Model-Guided Rubric Optimization for LLM Graders
author: Hongji Pu
Hang Li
Yucheng Chu
Jiliang Tang
abstract: Rubric optimization improves LLM grading by revising scoring instructions while keeping the grader's parameters fixed. Existing optimizers often judge edits by aggregate validation performance, limiting the supervision they retain about which errors an edit corrects or introduces. Testing each candidate also requires rescoring validation answers, which limits how many edits can be explored within a fixed budget. We propose RubricWorld, a framework that learns from previous edit evaluations to guide further search. Its world model predicts an edit's correction and degradation rates at score boundaries, conditioned on the current rubric state. The training signal comes from paired grading results: scores for the same answers before and after an edit. Predictions select one candidate for direct evaluation, and held-out confidence bounds determine whether it corrects enough target errors while keeping new errors within prespecified limits. Measured effects update the model even when the edit is rejected. Across EIR (National), ASAP2.0, and ASAP-SAS with three frozen LLM graders, RubricWorld achieves the highest score in 20 of 27 metric comparisons. On ASAP2.0, it raises gpt-5-mini accuracy from 18.20% with the original rubric to 46.70%, exceeding the strongest baseline, APO, by 22.60 percentage points. code will be released upon acceptance.

title: Synthetic Realities: Evaluating Human Ability to Distinguish AIGenerated Videos from Real Footage
author: Danyal Sarfraz
Raja Mubashar Karim
KwanMyung Kim
abstract: Recent advances in generative AI have enabled multiple pathways for high-fidelity video synthesis: text-to-video, image-to-video animation, and video outpainting. Empirical side-by-side evaluations of how untrained viewers perceive and distinguish these outputs from real footage remain scarce. In this study, we systematically compare human detection accuracy across these three AI generation techniques within three thematic contexts: historical footage, film and media content, and natural environments. We constructed a balanced stimulus set comprising equal amounts of real and AI-generated videos (18 each). The AI clips were evenly distributed across the three generation methods using Google's Veo 3, Lightricks LTX Video, and Wan VACE. All videos were produced and standardized within the ComfyUI framework to ensure consistent quality and duration. 87 participants judged every clip in a binary forced-choice task ("real" vs. "AI-generated"). Participants correctly identified videos 60% of the time on average. Image-to-video clips were recognized most accurately (79%), followed by real footage (64%), outpainting (49%), and text-to-video (43%). Accuracy also varied by theme: film and historical scenes yielded higher detection rates than environmental clips, which were frequently mistaken for AI. Logistic regression confirmed significant effects of both technique and theme as well as their interaction (p < 0.001), indicating that detection success depends jointly on how the content was generated and what it depicts. Findings reveal a consistent bias toward assuming synthetic origins and highlight that perceptual realism in AI video is shaped more by context than by model type, underscoring the importance of media-literacy approaches and context-aware evaluation tools for navigating increasingly synthetic visual media.

title: Safety4DM: A Vision-Language Framework for Risk-Aware Dynamic Maps in Vehicle-Road-Cloud Collaborative Driving
author: Zhengshu Zhou
Shaoyu Wang
Lu Tao
Xinhui Hu
Jiaqi Gu
Tingting Zhao
abstract: Dynamic map (DM) is a core information infrastructure for vehicle-road-cloud (VRC) cooperative autonomous driving. It fuses perception data from multiple sources to overcome the inherent line-of-sight and field-of-view limits of single-vehicle perception. However, DM still falls short on driving safety in two ways. First, DM data specifications already define road conditions semantically, but no pipeline yet turns real-world road observations into fine-grained risk entities in the DM. Second, existing DM systems lack a natural language interface for driving risks. To close these gaps, we propose Safety4DM, a safety-oriented language system for VRC dynamic maps. We first build RoadRisk, a real-world road image dataset that covers four types of road conditions and four risk levels. On this dataset, we fine-tune a vision-language model (VLM) for road safety risk perception. The model outputs structured risk representations that the DM can ingest directly. We then introduce a Safety-aware Step-wise Prompting (SafeStep) mechanism as the natural language query interface of the DM. SafeStep answers queries accurately and also generates actionable driving advice. To build and evaluate this interface, we develop SafeVRC-Sim, a VRC cooperative simulation framework, and SafeDM-QA, a safety question-answering benchmark. Experiments show that even the compact Qwen3-VL-4B reaches 89.83% accuracy on risk perception after fine-tuning. SafeStep also plugs easily into multiple LLM families. With medium and large models (20B and above) from five families, it achieves over 93% natural language query accuracy in every case, which shows strong generalization.

title: TrackMem: Tracking Evolving Beliefs in Long-Horizon Financial Dialogue
author: Austin M.Y. Cheung
Harsh Vardhan Gupta
Go Nam Lui
Lok Kan Chan
Ginny Y. Wong
Simon See
abstract: Memory systems for LLM agents are evaluated mostly on social dialogue, where facts accumulate and rarely change, so remembering reduces largely to finding the turn in which something was said. Financial dialogue breaks this assumption: figures are revised, stances shift without being restated, rules stated once govern later questions, and a single company is discussed under several analytical lenses. Memory systems that retrieve the passages most similar to a question, or the most recent ones, therefore return superseded values, miss rules that share no wording with the question, and cannot recover a stance spread across sessions. We present TrackMem, a per-speaker graph memory that tracks the history of figures, separates perspectives by entity and lens, and preserves each speaker's actions in chronological order. To evaluate it, we introduce FinLoCoMo, a benchmark of 15 long-horizon investment conversations with 765 questions in two splits: one following the LoCoMo categories and one targeting four failure modes. With two readers, TrackMem outperforms existing memory systems on both splits. On the failure-mode split it reaches 73.9% macro accuracy against 69.4% for the strongest baseline, with the largest gains on questions about revised figures (86.5% against 73.4%).

title: To Align Long, Plan Short: Simulating Diverse Profile-Aligned Students by Realizing Short-Term Plans in Long-Horizon Learning Environments
author: Bahar Radmehr
Jiaxu Zhao
Fatma BetÃ¼l GÃ¼reÅ
Adish Singla
Tanja KÃ¤ser
abstract: Simulated students offer a scalable way to test learning platforms and AI tutors before deployment with real students and to augment scarce data for studying learning at scale. Existing LLM-based simulators primarily target short, language-centered interactions. In open-ended learning environments, however, student behavior emerges from patterns across long-horizon interaction trajectories, where turn-level prompting can drift from an assigned behavior profile. We introduce ALPS (Align Long-term by Planning Short-term), a hierarchical simulated student conditioned on observable, environment-specific behavior profiles. Rather than selecting every action independently, ALPS alternates between planning profile-aligned task segments and generating the corresponding actions. We evaluate ALPS in both data-sufficient and data-scarce settings, where supervision comes either from real student trajectories or from a teacher LLM. Across both settings, we compare in-context learning (ICL), supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reward-ranked fine-tuning (RAFT), and their sequential combination (SFT followed by RAFT). Experiments in an inquiry-based physics game and a pharmacy simulation evaluate behavioral density and coverage against held-out real data, and profile consistency using a human-aligned LLM judge. Across both settings, ALPS consistently outperforms turn-level generation, achieving comparable density and judge pass rates under scarce supervision, although coverage remains lower. These results show that hierarchical planning enables faithful, profile-aligned simulation over long interaction horizons, even with limited real student data.

title: NAS-PO: Native Attention-Strategy Policy Optimization for Vision-Language Models
author: Ke An
Shizhe Xiang
Yue Liu
Liang Chen
Pei Fu
Shaojie Zhang
Xiaoxing Hu
Yupei Wang
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become an effective post-training paradigm for vision-language models (VLMs). Standard RLVR, however, assigns identical outcome-derived credit to all generated tokens regardless of their perceptual relevance. Recent perception-aware methods estimate visual reliance through image perturbation or masking. These indirect proxies require perturbation branches, while corruption sensitivity does not necessarily identify the visual evidence used for reasoning. We instead shape model perception through native attention, an intrinsic model signal. Rather than treating attention as a post-hoc explanation, we formulate it as a reward-anchored, token-aligned routing signal that encourages attention patterns supporting visually grounded reasoning. To this end, we propose NAS-PO, a Native Attention-Strategy Policy Optimization framework. NAS-PO analyzes native attention with a visual mass policy that quantifies visual allocation and a conditional visual policy that captures spatial routing over visual tokens, making the optimization well-posed. Based on this, Native Attention-Strategy Advantage Shaping (NAS-AS) draws on the visual-mass policy to redistribute signed policy-gradient credit for visually engaged rollouts. The Adaptive Attention-Coupled (AAC) loss then aligns the visual-mass policy on all response tokens and the conditional visual policy on visually active ones, consolidating the visual-routing patterns that drive successful trajectories. Experiments demonstrate that NAS-PO substantially surpasses leading RL-tuned VLMs across 7 out-of-domain reasoning and perception benchmarks, with its effectiveness consistently validated across 8B and 32B. Visual-Routing Sensitivity (VRS) analysis further indicates that the optimized attention prioritizes visually load-bearing regions.

title: Retrieval-Enhanced Cultural Evaluation for Social Media Translation Training
author: Linjuan Wu
Yiwen Qiu
Xinze Lyu
Dingming Li
Hui Yao
Zhongyi Sang
Ye Guo
Daoxin Zhang
Zhe Xu
Fei zhao
Mu Chuan
Yao Hu
Weiming Lu
Yongliang Shen
abstract: Social media translation requires preserving meaning while capturing the cultural nuances of user-generated content (UGC). However, gaps in the cultural knowledge of LLM-based evaluators can lead to inaccurate assessments and unreliable training rewards. To improve these signals, we use retrieval-enhanced cultural evaluation to train CUE-MT, a family of social media translation models. A calibrated, domain-specific Judger guides supervised data refinement and is augmented by an Agent for hard-example mining and reinforcement learning. The Agent retrieves relevant external evidence as needed and distills it into concise hints that the Judger uses to score translations and assign rewards. Across 9B, 27B, and 35B-A3B backbones, CUE-MT outperforms the evaluated open-source baselines of comparable size on CUE-MT-Bench and three public benchmarks. Human evaluation on CUE-MT-Bench shows cultural effectiveness gains of 7.44-15.12 percentage points over the strongest external baseline in each size group. Retrieval improves the Judger's four-way classification accuracy by 8.07 percentage points over a matched no-retrieval baseline that uses LLM-generated hints alone. Training ablations further support the combination of hard-example mining and Agent-enhanced rewards.

title: ClickSight: An LLM Framework for Interpreting Student Clickstreams Through Learning Strategies
author: Bahar Radmehr
Lan Tran
Ekaterina Shved
Fatma Bet{Ã¼}l G{Ã¼}reÅ
Adish Singla
Tanja K{Ã¤}ser
abstract: Digital learning environments produce rich clickstream data that can reveal how students approach learning tasks, yet interpreting these fine-grained traces often requires substantial expert effort. We introduce ClickSight, a framework for interpreting student clickstreams through learning strategies defined in the literature. Given a student clickstream and a predefined set of learning strategies, ClickSight uses a staged LLM-based pipeline to identify strategy-relevant evidence, assess adherence to each strategy, and generate an evidence-grounded interpretation of the student's behavior. We evaluate ClickSight across two learning environments, 365 students, and 12 model backbones using an expert-grounded quality rubric and an LLM judge calibrated with human-expert ratings. Our results show that ClickSight can generate high-quality strategy-based interpretations across different models and environments, with reasoning models performing more consistently than instruction-tuned counterparts. We further find that providing external clickstream-extracted guidance can improve interpretation quality for strategies that require precise quantitative information from the trace. By connecting fine-grained clickstreams with theoretically defined learning strategies and preserving the evidence underlying each judgment, ClickSight provides a flexible approach for studying student behavior in digital learning environments.

title: Reconstruction as Spatial Evaluation: Diagnosing Cross-View Spatial Intelligence in Large Vision-Language Models
author: Junfei Wu
Qiuyue Wang
Xuhong Huang
Qihang Peng
Mingsheng Li
Jian Guan
Qiang Liu
Shu Wu
Liang Wang
Shuai Bai
Tieniu Tan
abstract: The spatial intelligence of large vision-language models (LVLMs) requires the ability to combine local visual observations into a geometrically consistent representation of the physical world. Many static benchmarks assess isolated spatial judgments, such as relative direction or distance, while interactive embodied evaluations combine perception with exploration, planning, control, and simulator-specific execution. To bridge this gap, we introduce RECONSPATIAL, a benchmark centered on multi-view 3D scene reconstruction across indoor, tabletop, and outdoor environments. Given real multi-view images and target-object queries, LVLMs are required to jointly predict oriented 3D bounding boxes in a shared, camera-anchored metric coordinate frame. Reconstructions are evaluated along two complementary axes: Structure for relative layout and Metric for physical scale and camera-anchored placement. Nine atomic spatial QA tasks, grouped into Geometric Perception and Spatial Relations, probe spatial capabilities involved in joint reconstruction. Offline navigation extends evaluation to path planning. Evaluation of 18 frontier LVLMs reveals a consistent gap between relative scene structure and metric reconstruction; even GPT-6-Astra scores 81.4% on Structure but only 58.7% on Metric. Tracing this gap, diagnostic analyses link atomic spatial capabilities to reconstruction quality and show that relational consistency alone does not ensure metric accuracy. Experiments with 3D map injection further separate scene construction from path planning, revealing how these geometric errors limit navigation success. Finally, spatial fine-tuning yields broad transfer across both spatial and general vision-language benchmarks.

title: LARK: Lean-Assisted Reasoning for LLM-Generated GPU Kernels
author: Zixi Zhang
Jiayi Nie
Haoran Wu
Yujie Yan
Yann Herklotz
Rika Antonova
Robert Mullins
Yiren Zhao
George A. Constantinides
Jianyi Cheng
abstract: Efficient GPU kernels are typically low-level and hardware-specific, and LLM agents can now generate them faster than experts can verify. Existing approaches rely on testing, which provides evidence but not a guarantee of correctness. We introduce LARK, an agentic framework that automatically and formally verifies GPU kernels against their PyTorch reference implementations. LARK proves equivalence in functional and memory behavior under exact arithmetic and establishes a new trust boundary: human effort is only needed to verify operator-level Lean semantics ahead of kernel generation time, instead of checking every single line of generated code. LARK formalizes the GPU machine model and the semantics of each operation in Lean 4 once per target language, and the Lean 4 semantics of any incoming kernel is derived from these pre-built definitions. LLM agents then automate the proof in two steps. First, an agent decomposes the whole kernel semantics into smaller segments and Lean 4 verifies this segmentation, which addresses the intractability of proving equivalence for large kernels directly. Second, agents write Lean proofs that each kernel segment matches its high-level PyTorch counterpart. Together, the two steps give whole-program equivalence. We demonstrate that LARK can be used 1) to ensure correctness in existing code-generation agents and 2) to automatically verify human-written kernel libraries. On the KernelCraft GPU tasks, combined with a simple ReAct agent, LARK enables GLM 5.3 to fully verify 10 of 12 Level-1 kernels and Opus 5.5 all 5 Level-2 kernels. Moreover, over 10 production kernels randomly sampled from popular open-source LLM serving frameworks, LARK verifies 9 and identifies a new data race bug in the tenth. We believe LARK represents a significant step toward verifiable code generation in the agentic era.

title: PRISM: RL-Based Rate Control for Low Latency and High Data Rate in Mobile Edge Networks
author: Hamid Hassani
Staji Wilson
Kishor C. Joshi
Sonia M. Heemstra
Ignas G. Niemegeers
George Exarchakos
abstract: Emerging delay-sensitive interactive services, such as extended reality and remote operation, demand advanced congestion control algorithms (CCAs) capable of maintaining high data rates while keeping latency low in mobile networks. Existing CCAs typically rely on congestion signals such as packet loss, delay, or explicit congestion notification (ECN) marks, which can be delayed, imprecise, or require extensive upgrades to the network infrastructure. To address these limitations, physical resource block (PRB) utilization has recently been proposed as a reliable early congestion signal in mobile networks [1]. This paper introduces PRISM, a reinforcement-learning-based CCA that uses peak PRB utilization to regulate the send rate under challenging mobility and fading conditions. NS3 simulation results show that, in a mobility scenario where two PRISM flows coexist with two TCP Cubic flows and one TCP BBR flow, PRISM maintains a per-packet mean one-way delay (OWD) of 6.3ms and a $p_{99}$ OWD of 44.6ms, with negligible (0.02%) packet loss, over a 20min high-contention interval. However, over the same interval, the coexisting TCP flows experience 60x higher mean OWDs of 371-390ms and $p_{99}$ OWDs of 563-578ms, with 0.1% packet loss. PRISM achieves a 31x improvement in goodput-over-latency performance, indicating a favorable tradeoff for delay-sensitive applications.

title: How Green Is Your Manifesto? Scoring Environmental Positions in the 2024 EU Elections with an LLM Panel
author: Franco Corti
Sajid Siraj
abstract: Locating political parties on environmental and climate policy is central to the study of party competition, yet the established instruments, expert surveys and the hand coding of manifestos, are costly, periodic, and slow to extend to new documents. We ask whether a panel of large language models can serve as a cheaper and reproducible alternative. Treating each manifesto as a set of sentences, three models from independent providers score every sentence on two dimensions, environmental protection and climate change, separating a party's position on an issue from the salience it gives it, and the judgments are averaged to the manifesto level. Agreement across the models is retained as a built-in reliability signal. We apply the panel to 41 manifestos from the 2024 European Parliament election, covering Austria, France, Germany, Italy, Spain, and the European party families, and validate it against the 2024 Chapel Hill Expert Survey for the 25 parties with a like-for-like expert benchmark, using the other manifestos as diagnostic cases. The panel recovers the expert ordering of parties with strong rank agreement on both dimensions, while reading them as systematically greener than experts do, a gap we interpret as the distance between manifesto promise and governing record. Inter-model disagreement modestly flags where the instrument errs, and position and salience prove related for environmental protection but independent for climate change. The result is a transparent, low-cost, and multilingual instrument that complements rather than replaces expert and hand-coded approaches; the prompt, code, and manifesto-level results are released openly.

title: Scalar Smoothness Is One Point on a Besov Spectrum
author: Bum Jun Kim
Anastasis Kratsios
abstract: Studies of neural network generalization and robustness often summarize smoothness with a single number, such as a Lipschitz constant or a Hessian curvature statistic. However, Lipschitz constants summarize global worst-case sensitivity and Hessian statistics summarize local curvature; neither captures how model responses vary with the size, direction, and location of perturbations encountered in real-world deployment. To measure smoothness under these perturbations, we introduce a finite-difference roughness spectrum that profiles model responses across these conditions. Our roughness spectrum generalizes scalar smoothness measures, bringing Lipschitz sensitivity and directional Hessian curvature into a common framework across perturbation scales. We connect this spectrum to classical Besov theory, which describes how a function's variation changes with scale. Our theoretical analysis also proves that a larger output shift can cause less task damage than a smaller one, and that local curvature alone can miss the blocks most vulnerable to finite perturbations. In image classification, Roughness Source Control (RSC) suppresses margin roughness along noise directions and improves noise robustness in a comparison of 80 checkpoints across four model--dataset combinations. In post-training quantization, we identify blocks that need higher precision by measuring task-loss increases from perturbations matched to the size and direction of each block's quantization error. Our mixed-precision allocation achieves lower perplexity than the Hessian-based HAWQ-V2 baseline under the same GPTQ weights and bit budgets in all 14 settings across seven held-out large language models.

title: Unified Loss-Aware Density Control for 3D Gaussian Splatting
author: Tae-Young Kim
Jiwoo Chung
Jae-Pil Heo
abstract: The efficiency and fidelity of 3D Gaussian Splatting critically depend on adaptive density control, which grows and suppresses Gaussian primitives throughout optimization. However, the standard pipeline still relies on heuristic view-space gradients, scale thresholds, and global opacity resets, rather than explicitly assessing the loss-reducing effect of each split, clone, or opacity update. This mismatch can allocate primitives to already-sufficient regions, miss under-reconstructed structures, and destabilize training through blanket opacity changes. In this work, we recast adaptive density control as a collection of local loss-reduction decisions. We derive efficient Taylor-based per-Gaussian surrogates that predict the objective change caused by three primitive-level operations: splitting, cloning, and opacity decay. This yields a unified loss-aware framework with three components. First, we extend second-order splitting to a normalized joint position-scale space, enabling children to adapt not only their locations but also their anisotropic extents. Second, we formulate duplicate cloning as a surrogate minimization problem, selecting only Gaussians whose duplicated contribution is predicted to improve reconstruction and assigning each child a principled opacity. Third, we replace global opacity reset with selective soft opacity decay that weakens harmful primitives while preserving useful ones. Across standard 3DGS benchmarks, our method produces more targeted primitive allocation and achieves improved rendering quality with comparable or smaller Gaussian budgets compared to baselines.

title: Beliefs in feedback: Factored representations of interacting agents in transformers
author: David A. Ehrlich
Manuel Baltieri
Fernando E. Rosas
Alexander B. Boyd
abstract: Complex systems, from ecosystems to brains, are usually modeled as modular components coupled through feedback rather than as indivisible wholes. Can a transformer trained on the joint behavior of a group of interacting agents be understood in the same way? In this work, we develop a computational-mechanics framework to study agents interacting in feedback loops. We formally prove that any joint stochastic process can be presented as resulting from the behavior of agents interacting in feedback, and the resulting process is generated by a hidden Markov model whose Bayesian beliefs factorize into separate components per agent. Furthermore, our experiments show that transformers trained on such feedback sequences make use of this separability, disentangling the beliefs about the underlying factors into separate subspaces of their residual stream. This representation is found to scale linearly (instead of exponentially) with the number of agents. Moreover, interventions show that these representations are causally efficacious, allowing for targeted steering of individual agents' beliefs by selectively inserting counterfactuals. However, coarse-graining the behavior is found to disrupt the factorization, and can force a higher-dimensional representation. Together, the results establish both the dimensional advantage of a factorized representation and the ability of transformers to exploit it, laying the groundwork for investigating traces of compositional predictive architecture in pretrained models.

title: UniGS-SLAM: Monocular Gaussian SLAM with Enhanced Geometry and Open-Vocabulary Semantics
author: Xingyuan Ding
Sicheng Yu
Kaiyong Zhao
Hao Wang
abstract: Monocular semantic SLAM aims to reconstruct scene geometry and build semantic maps from RGB observations. Existing Gaussian-based methods often attach semantic labels or features to evolving Gaussian primitives, making semantic fusion difficult to maintain and increasing reconstruction overhead. Hybrid Gaussian--voxel representations provide more stable semantic support, but often rely on RGB-D input or known poses and do not revise historical semantic evidence after geometry updates. We present UniGS-SLAM, an RGB-only framework that decouples open-vocabulary semantics from Gaussian reconstruction while preserving bidirectional interaction. Foundation priors enhance monocular depth and pose estimation, while semantic observations are fused into an independent sparse voxel map with observation provenance, enabling historical contributions to be revised as reconstruction evolves. The fused semantics further guide Gaussian filtering and local surface refinement. Experiments on Replica, ScanNet, and KITTI-360 show leading tracking, rendering, and geometric reconstruction performance among representative RGB-only methods, together with strong open-set semantic mapping on Replica and ScanNet. We also achieve a 2.37-fold reconstruction speedup over the fastest compared semantic SLAM baseline. Project page: https://3dagentworld.github.io/UniGS-SLAM/.

title: Same Function, Different Gradients: Evaluating Gradient Reliability under Reparameterization
author: Bum Jun Kim
abstract: Gradients are no longer used only to train models: Gradient magnitudes are now measurement instruments, used to rank attention heads for pruning, to decide per-example clipping in private training, to allocate adapter rank budgets, and to debug models. Across these workflows, larger gradient magnitudes are taken to mean greater importance. Even for a fixed input--output function, these gradients are computed in one of many possible parameter coordinate systems. For example, attention scores depend on the query and key projections only through the paired product $W_QW_K^\top$. Scaling a head's query projection by $c$ and the corresponding key projection by $1/c$ therefore leaves every output logit unchanged. This change in parameter coordinates rescales the corresponding query and key gradient norms by $1/c$ and $c$, respectively. To test whether gradient-based decisions remain unchanged under these coordinate changes, we introduce Gradient Reliability under Reparameterization (GRR). GRR rewrites a trained model in new parameter coordinates that compute exactly the same function, verifies that predictions are unchanged, and then tests whether the decisions derived from the gradients are unchanged too. Our audits span GLUE classifiers, a ViT on CIFAR-10, GPT-2-medium and GPT-2-large, a 1.1B-parameter Llama-style model on WikiText-2, and six trained LoRA adapters. Empirically, predictions are preserved throughout, but both the gradients and the gradient-based decisions change. Across 66 GLUE attention audits, the median top-3 overlap of raw head-gradient rankings is only $1/3$, and rankings and pruning masks change even under the mildest rescalings we test. In the largest of 14 global-pruning audits, the shifted ranking selects head masks that differ in four of 22 pruned heads and reach $50.92\%$ and $94.84\%$ validation accuracy on one ELECTRA SST-2 model.

title: Learning to Look: A Foundation for Visual Understanding
author: Wenshuai Zhao
Yihao Wang
Benjamin Robson
Juho Kannala
Arno Solin
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) suffer from visual hallucination, such as saying an object that is not present in an image. We ask a more fundamental question: whether a VLM is even aware of where it is looking before understanding the semantic meaning in the image. We formulate this question as a LOOK task: identifying which parts of its visual input were available to the model. We construct the task in a self-supervised way without manually labeling the available region to the model. Our experiments show that existing VLMs fail to localize the visible region. We further show that fine-tuning VLMs on the proposed LOOK task improves a model's awareness of visual input.

title: Do Embodied VLMs Actually Use Their Scene-Graph Memory?
author: Shubh Garg
Divyansh Pandey
Vedant Khandelwal
Niyati Rawal
Amit Sheth
abstract: Embodied agents that answer questions about their route need a memory of what they saw, and scene graphs are a natural form for it. A vision-language model (VLM) can receive such a graph as text or through a graph encoder, but accuracy alone cannot show whether the graph holds the episode's facts, reaches the model, or is actually relied on. In this diagnostic study, we introduce a graph-swap test for the last of these: each episode is given another episode's graph, and we count how many answers change. On an embodied question-answering benchmark with routes through two to seven rooms, we use it to compare ways of delivering scene-graph memory to a fine-tuned VLM. As text, the memory is used strongly, adding 30 points on route questions. As a graph, it is not, and we trace why: the encoder preserves the information, but standard pooled and late fusion discard it. Giving each node its own input token recovers part of it, a gain of 8.3 points on route questions that the swap test confirms comes from the graph. The test also exposes a shortcut that accuracy hides: when the same facts appear in the text, the model ignores its graph. The test thus offers a cheap check of whether a VLM uses its scene-graph memory, and our analysis points to how that memory should be delivered.

title: Fragility Is Not Reducible to Hardness: Conditional Causal Difficulty for LLMs
author: Mohammad Reza Rezaei
Dingxian Wang
Nikhil Verma
Sajjad Pakdamansavoji
Andrew Rabinovich
Zhao Chen
abstract:
Large language models show large and seemingly arbitrary performance drops when a task is rewritten in ways that leave its requirements untouched. We recast task difficulty as a causal quantity: the treatment effect of meaning-preserving perturbations on a model. A meaning-preserving rewrite can only be observed to hurt a task the model can already solve, so we place the estimand on the principal stratum where the degradation occurs: the conditional causal difficulty (CCD), the probability that a randomly drawn twin breaks a solvable task. Because harder tasks tend to be more phrasing-sensitive, complexity enters as an effect modifier rather than a confounder, and we residualize it out to obtain complexity-residualized difficulty (CRD); zero for a task exactly as fragile as its complexity predicts, positive for anomalously fragile ones. Current benchmarks do not supply the data CCD requires, so we introduce GlassGSM and GlassMATH, augmenting GSM8K and MATH with twins built from perturbation families, raising fragility on GlassGSM by $\approx 12\times$ over GSM-IC-style distractors on the same problems ($3.7\%\to44.9\%$) while keeping the answer key unchanged. Our predictor Frail learns the per-perturbation break probability and reaches $0.613{\pm}0.023$ of the suite reliability ceiling on GlassGSM and $0.557{\pm}0.023$ on GlassMATH, against $0.171$/$0.401$ for a surface-feature baseline and $0.444$/$0.463$ for supervised baselines such as VAP3, and, at a $5\%$ curation budget on GlassGSM, doubles random recall of fragile items, matching an oracle ranking. Additionally, cross-fitted residualization leaves CRD uncorrelated with the declared proxy in practice.
Code is available at https://github.com/upwork/Conditional_Causal_Difficulty_for_LLMs

title: State-Aware Virtual Patient Simulation for Training Psychiatrists in Challenging Clinical Scenarios
author: Harsh Mohta
C Chandrahas Reddy
Sunhith Reddy Bojja
Manik Inder Singh Sethi
Vinesh Gupta
Raghuram Bharadwaj Diddigi
abstract: Psychiatrists must be prepared to manage patients exhibiting challenging psychological states, including suicidal ideation, hallucinations, and other high-risk behaviors. However, opportunities to safely practice such interactions are limited. While recent conversational agents can simulate patients, existing approaches largely rely on large language models (LLMs) to determine patient responses, making it difficult to consistently maintain psychological state, adapt to the clinician's responses, and generate clinically plausible challenges that meaningfully test the clinician. We present a state-aware virtual patient simulation pipeline for training psychiatrists in challenging clinical scenarios. The proposed system maintains an evolving patient state throughout the interaction and orchestrates patient behavior rather than leaving response generation entirely to an LLM. At each interaction, a learning-based behavioral strategy selector determines the type and level of challenge appropriate to the current patient and clinician context. The selected strategy, patient state, clinician response, interaction history, and relevant clinical knowledge are then provided as grounded context to an LLM to generate a semantically relevant and psychologically consistent patient response. Following each session, the system analyzes the interaction and provides feedback to the clinician on their communication and management of the virtual patient.

title: Scene-Adaptive Readout and Decoding in Diffusion Driving VLAs
author: Seungjun Yu
Jiho Choi
Inha Kang
Hojun Choi
Seungwook Kim
Hyunjung Shim
abstract: Diffusion driving vision-language-action models repeatedly execute the backbone at every denoising stage, incurring substantial inference cost, while it remains unclear whether all scenes require the same decoding computation. To distinguish when a trajectory becomes readable from how much further refinement it requires, we analyze trajectory readout across network depth and decoding progress. We identify a depth-decoding dissociation in which late-layer representations already support useful trajectory readout after the first forward sweep, whereas early-layer representations benefit more from continued decoding. We further find that both the preferred readout layer and decoding depth vary across scenes. Based on these observations, we propose a scene-adaptive readout and decoding framework. A scene-conditioned readout MoE adaptively weights and combines trajectory predictions from layer-specific late-layer representations after a single backbone sweep, while an adaptive decoding policy applies additional native refinement only when required by the scene. We evaluate our framework on two diffusion driving VLAs across the Waymo E2E and nuScenes benchmarks. Our method improves validation RFS by up to 0.56 while also improving test performance, and achieves an end-to-end speedup of up to $6.0\times$ on Waymo E2E, while consistently reducing trajectory error on nuScenes. These results demonstrate that scene-level readout and decoding allocation improves planning quality while avoiding unnecessary decoding. Our code is available at https://github.com/sjyu001/SARD

title: ParetoSaddler: Pareto-Guided Optimization of Agent Harnesses for Quality and Cost
author: Xingzhi Qian
Sungho Park
Rongyuan Tan
Jianbo Yu
Jue Zhang
Lorenzo Cavallaro
Menglin Xia
Yanzhi Chen
Xinnuo Xu
Yu Kang
Xinran Zheng
Gagan Somashekar
Xuchao Zhang
Chetan Bansal
Qingwei Lin
Victor RÃ¼hle
abstract: Harness optimization can substantially improve LLM agents without modifying model weights, but existing methods primarily optimize response quality. Extending them to joint quality--cost optimization introduces a challenge: applying the deployment preference during intermediate updates can prematurely reject candidates that are valuable for later improvements. We introduce ParetoSaddler, which addresses this mismatch by separating intermediate candidate promotion from final deployment selection. At each iteration, an optimizer updates a parent harness to produce a candidate, and then compares the two over repeated executions and uses Bayesian bootstrap Pareto support to promote candidates showing credible progress in either quality or cost. Promoted candidates receive broader development evaluation and remain available as parents for later optimization steps. We evaluate ParetoSaddler on ClawMark and GAIA2 using domain-disjoint splits. On ClawMark, ParetoSaddler improves quality from 70.86\% to 81.35\% while reducing cost from \$1.17 to \$1.01 per task; on GAIA2, it improves quality from 56.22\% to 62.89\% while reducing cost from \$0.78 to \$0.45 per task. The Pareto-selected harnesses also achieve higher quality at lower cost than quality-only harness optimization. Analysis shows that Pareto-aware optimization retains intermediate candidates that would be discarded by deployment preference but can support later improvements, while Bayesian bootstrap screening filters out candidates whose gains are weakly supported across runs.

title: Fairway: Load-Aware KV Cache Reuse for LLM Prefill Scheduling
author: Hamidreza Alikhani
Nazmul Takbir
Matin Khajavi
Rajat Bhattacharjya
Sangeetha Abdu Jyothi
Nikil Dutt
abstract: LLM-based applications often employ agentic workflows and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which build long prompts from shared context. When prefixes are shared across requests, serving engines reuse the key-value (KV) cache to skip parts of the prefill computation. Reuse is typically graded: the uncached work of requests in a queue can differ by up to 100x. In this setting, the order of scheduling determines the time-to-first-token (TTFT) for the queued requests. KV reuse-first scheduling, which prioritizes the requests with the longest KV cache hit, gives the lowest median TTFT but starves expensive requests under load spikes; first-come-first-served (FCFS) scheduling bounds the tail but raises the median TTFT. We present Fairway, a prefill scheduler built on adaptive reuse prioritization: it favors KV cache reuse while queues are short, and shifts toward fair allocation as requests wait longer relative to their own prefill time. Fairway employs a virtual dual lane model: a KV reuse-first Fast lane and a Fair lane atop the serving engine's waiting queue that enables speeding up of cheap reuse requests without starving expensive ones. This model automatically adapts to the workload without any per-workload tuning. Fairway lowers the tail TTFT at no cost to the median in transient overload. Across workloads and load levels, Fairway matches or beats the best baseline, with a p99 TTFT up to 8.6x lower than prior prefix-aware schedulers. During load spikes, it keeps the tail of FCFS at a 6x lower median TTFT.

title: Measuring "Success" In the Transition from Pre- to Post-LLM Conversational Agents through the Lens of Interaction & Explanations for Older Adults
author: Tamara Zubatiy
Niharika Mathur
Reina Chan
Srijan Pokharel
Rosemarie Santa GonzÃ¡lez
Agata Rozga
Xiang Zhi Tan
Elizabeth D. Mynatt
abstract: Conversational agents (CAs) for older adults have moved through at least two distinct eras, split by the emergence of large language models (LLMs) at the end of 2022. The first era was defined by commercial smart speakers such as the original Google Home and Amazon Alexa, built on rigid, rule-based dialogue. Interactions were single-turn, user-initiated and "successful" if and only if a command matched one of a finite set of pre-templated intents. The current era is marked by LLM-powered systems capable of open-ended, multi-turn conversation, with capacity for personalization and foundations for more proactive interaction. This shift has not only transformed what CAs can do for users, but also changed what researchers can measure when it comes to understanding "success" of user interactions with CAs. In this case study, we reflect on over 8 years of research spanning more than 100 participants across multiple field sites to trace how our own working definitions of "success" have evolved. We reflect on two completed bodies of work with pre-LLM CAs and an in-progress study with a post-LLM CA. We discuss how our definition and measurement of success have evolved during this transition and also ask open questions to the community about how to optimally measure "success" in the post-LLM CA era. This research is deeply applied and subject to the messiness of real-world deployments. Our intended contributions are deliberately practical, a combination of methodological considerations and reflection questions to support researchers engaging with this new wave of technologies.

title: Local Solution Repair for Multi-Agent Pickup and Delivery
author: Ethan Schneider
Jingkai Chen
Seth Hutchinson
Sonia Chernova
abstract: Multi-robot systems in automated warehouses must efficiently attend to a constant stream of pickup-and-delivery tasks while avoiding collisions. Existing Multi-Agent Pickup-and-Delivery (MAPD) solutions generate plans that are globally feasible but often locally inefficient. In large-scale, long-horizon deployments, these inefficiencies, such as robots backtracking from target goal locations and idling in congested areas, accumulate over time and degrade performance. This paper contributes Local Solution Repair (LSR), a goal replanning approach that detects suboptimal behaviors at run-time and locally improves plans to reduce conflict between agents. We demonstrate the utility of our approach by repairing solutions generated by state-of-the-art MAPD baselines, M2M and LNS-PBS. Our results in long-horizon warehouse simulations over three environments show upwards of 5.9% improvement in task throughput over current state-of-the-art methods by reducing the number of suboptimal instances by ~36k or by 14.6% with minor additional computation time.

title: HQNN-CL: Regime-Aware Hybrid Quantum Neural Network with Continual Learning for Financial Forecasting
author: Muhammad Atif Saeed
Akhtar Jamil
Subhan Ullah
abstract: Financial time-series forecasting is still difficult owing to the non-stationary nature of the market, regime changes, and catastrophic forgetting, which makes conventional deep learning models hard to adapt in the long term. To achieve uncertainty-aware robust financial forecasting in the face of changing market conditions, this study proposes a Hybrid Quantum-Classical Neural Network with Continual Learning (HQNN-CL).
